claim: The integration of most membrane proteins into the cytoplasmic membrane of bacteria occurs co-translationally.
source: The integration of most membrane proteins into the cytoplasmic membrane of bacteria occurs co-translationally.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about bacterial membrane protein integration.

claim: The universally conserved YidC protein mediates membrane protein integration either individually as a membrane protein insertase, or in concert with the SecY complex.
source: The universally conserved YidC protein mediates this process either individually as a membrane protein insertase, or in concert with the SecY complex.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about YidC function.

claim: A structural model of YidC was developed based on evolutionary co-variation analysis, lipid-versus-protein-exposure and molecular dynamics simulations.
source: Here, we present a structural model of YidC based on evolutionary co-variation analysis, lipid-versus-protein-exposure and molecular dynamics simulations.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methods used to create the model.

claim: The YidC model suggests a distinctive arrangement of the conserved five transmembrane domains.
source: The model suggests a distinctive arrangement of the conserved five transmembrane domains and a helical hairpin between transmembrane segment 2 (TM2) and TM3 on the cytoplasmic membrane surface.
evidence: This is based on the structural modeling described in the manuscript.

claim: The YidC model includes a helical hairpin between transmembrane segment 2 (TM2) and TM3 on the cytoplasmic membrane surface.
source: The model suggests a distinctive arrangement of the conserved five transmembrane domains and a helical hairpin between transmembrane segment 2 (TM2) and TM3 on the cytoplasmic membrane surface.
evidence: This is based on the structural modeling described in the manuscript.

claim: The YidC model was docked into a cryo-electron microscopy reconstruction of a translating YidC-ribosome complex carrying the YidC substrate FOc.
source: The model was used for docking into a cryo-electron microscopy reconstruction of a translating YidC-ribosome complex carrying the YidC substrate FOc.
evidence: The manuscript describes the cryo-EM reconstruction and docking procedure.

claim: A single copy of YidC interacts with the ribosome at the ribosomal tunnel exit.
source: This structure reveals how a single copy of YidC interacts with the ribosome at the ribosomal tunnel exit and identifies a site for membrane protein insertion at the YidC protein-lipid interface.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and analysis.

claim: A site for membrane protein insertion exists at the YidC protein-lipid interface.
source: This structure reveals how a single copy of YidC interacts with the ribosome at the ribosomal tunnel exit and identifies a site for membrane protein insertion at the YidC protein-lipid interface.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and analysis.

claim: High resolution structures are available only for the first periplasmic domain (P1) of Escherichia coli YidC.
source: High resolution structures are available only for the first periplasmic domain (P1) of Escherichia coli YidC (Figure 1A; Oliver and Paetzel, 2008; Ravaud et al., 2008), however, this domain is poorly conserved, only present in Gram-negative bacteria and not essential for functionality (Jiang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The P1 domain of YidC is poorly conserved, only present in Gram-negative bacteria and not essential for functionality.
source: High resolution structures are available only for the first periplasmic domain (P1) of Escherichia coli YidC (Figure 1A; Oliver and Paetzel, 2008; Ravaud et al., 2008), however, this domain is poorly conserved, only present in Gram-negative bacteria and not essential for functionality (Jiang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2003.

claim: The region(s) of YidC mediating the interaction with the ribosome have not been identified.
source: Furthermore, the region(s) of YidC mediating the interaction with the ribosome have not been identified, and the oligomeric state of YidC during co-translational translocation remains controversial (Kohler et al., 2009; Herrmann, 2013; Kedrov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge at the time of the study.

claim: The oligomeric state of YidC during co-translational translocation remains controversial.
source: Furthermore, the region(s) of YidC mediating the interaction with the ribosome have not been identified, and the oligomeric state of YidC during co-translational translocation remains controversial (Kohler et al., 2009; Herrmann, 2013; Kedrov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FOc is an integral membrane subunit of the ATP synthase complex.
source: Hence, we set out to determine a molecular model of ribosome-bound YidC during co-translational translocation of the substrate FOc (van der Laan et al., 2004), an integral membrane subunit of the ATP synthase complex.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van der Laan et al., 2004.

claim: A multiple sequence alignment of 2366 non-redundant YidC sequences was constructed excluding the unconserved first transmembrane helix (TM1) and the periplasmic P1 domain.
source: We constructed a multiple sequence alignment of E. coli YidC excluding the nonconserved first transmembrane helix (TM1) and the P1 domain (Figure 1A) and computed direct evolutionary couplings between pairs of YidC residues (Kamisetty et al., 2013).
evidence: This is described in the methods section of the manuscript.

claim: Direct evolutionary couplings between pairs of YidC residues were computed using the method of Kamisetty et al. (2013).
source: We constructed a multiple sequence alignment of E. coli YidC excluding the nonconserved first transmembrane helix (TM1) and the P1 domain (Figure 1A) and computed direct evolutionary couplings between pairs of YidC residues (Kamisetty et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the method used.

claim: Seven helix–helix contacts attained probabilities above 57%.
source: Seven helix–helix contacts attained probabilities above 57% (Figure 1B–D) while all other possible contacts scored below 15%, demonstrating the specificity of the method (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on the covariation analysis and shown in the figures.

claim: All other possible helix-helix contacts scored below 15% probability.
source: Seven helix–helix contacts attained probabilities above 57% (Figure 1B–D) while all other possible contacts scored below 15%, demonstrating the specificity of the method (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on the covariation analysis and shown in the figures.

claim: The conserved membrane integrated core of YidC forms a helical bundle arranged like the vertices of a pentagon, in the order 4-5-3-2-6 (clockwise) when viewed from the cytoplasm.
source: In the resulting model (Figure 1E,F), the conserved membrane integrated core of YidC forms a helical bundle arranged like the vertices of a pentagon, in the order 4-5-3-2-6 (clockwise) when viewed from the cytoplasm (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on the structural model shown in the figures.

claim: All the predicted interactions between TM domains can be explained by monomeric YidC.
source: Notably, all the predicted interactions between TM domains can be explained by monomeric YidC suggesting that dimer or oligomer formation may not be strictly required for YidC activity (see also below).
evidence: This is based on the covariation analysis and structural modeling.

claim: Dimer or oligomer formation may not be strictly required for YidC activity.
source: Notably, all the predicted interactions between TM domains can be explained by monomeric YidC suggesting that dimer or oligomer formation may not be strictly required for YidC activity (see also below).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural model.

claim: Strong helix–helix contacts were predicted within the cytoplasmic loop between TM2 and TM3, which can be explained by the formation of a helical hairpin.
source: Outside the membrane region, strong helix–helix contacts were predicted within the cytoplasmic loop between TM2 and TM3, which can be explained the by formation of a helical hairpin (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on the covariation analysis and structural modeling.

claim: The base of the helical paddle domain (HPD) is structurally constrained by predicted contacts with TM3.
source: The base of this 'helical paddle domain' (HPD) is structurally constrained by predicted contacts with TM3, its tip on the other hand is more mobile and appears to interact with lipid headgroups (see below).
evidence: This is based on the covariation analysis and structural modeling.

claim: The tip of the helical paddle domain is more mobile and appears to interact with lipid headgroups.
source: The base of this 'helical paddle domain' (HPD) is structurally constrained by predicted contacts with TM3, its tip on the other hand is more mobile and appears to interact with lipid headgroups (see below).
evidence: This is based on the structural modeling and MD simulations.

claim: Two crystal structures of Bacillus halodurans YidC2 (BhYidC2, 34% sequence identity with E. coli YidC) were published while this manuscript was under review.
source: While this manuscript was under review, two crystal structures were published of Bacillus halodurans YidC2 (BhYidC2, 34% sequence identity with E. coli YidC) (Kumazaki et al., 2014), providing us with a unique opportunity to directly assess the accuracy of our model.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kumazaki et al., 2014.

claim: The root mean square deviation (RMSD) between the TM helices of the E. coli YidC model and those of BhYidC2 is 7.5 Å (3WO6) and 7.3 Å (3WO7).
source: Overall, the root mean square deviation (RMSD) between the TM helices of our model and those of BhYidC2 is 7.5 Å (3WO6) and 7.3 Å (3WO7) (Table 1), which is within the resolution limits of our method.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the model to the crystal structures.

claim: The RMSD between the TM helices of the E. coli YidC model and BhYidC2 is within the resolution limits of the covariation method.
source: Overall, the root mean square deviation (RMSD) between the TM helices of our model and those of BhYidC2 is 7.5 Å (3WO6) and 7.3 Å (3WO7) (Table 1), which is within the resolution limits of our method.
evidence: This is an assessment of the model accuracy.

claim: The global arrangement of TM helices in the E. coli YidC model is the same as in BhYidC2.
source: The global arrangement of TM helices is the same as in BhYidC2, yet, their tilt angle relative to the plane of the membrane is slightly different (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the model to the crystal structures.

claim: The tilt angle of TM helices relative to the plane of the membrane is slightly different between the E. coli YidC model and BhYidC2.
source: The global arrangement of TM helices is the same as in BhYidC2, yet, their tilt angle relative to the plane of the membrane is slightly different (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the model to the crystal structures.

claim: The tilt angle of the HPD differs between the E. coli YidC model and BhYidC2.
source: The tilt angle of the HPD also differs, as well as its side that faces the membrane (Video 1), which may be indicative of a high degree of flexibility of this domain, consistent with its high crystallographic B-factors (Kumazaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the model to the crystal structures.

claim: The side of the HPD that faces the membrane differs between the E. coli YidC model and BhYidC2.
source: The tilt angle of the HPD also differs, as well as its side that faces the membrane (Video 1), which may be indicative of a high degree of flexibility of this domain, consistent with its high crystallographic B-factors (Kumazaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the model to the crystal structures.

claim: The differences in HPD orientation may be indicative of a high degree of flexibility of this domain.
source: The tilt angle of the HPD also differs, as well as its side that faces the membrane (Video 1), which may be indicative of a high degree of flexibility of this domain, consistent with its high crystallographic B-factors (Kumazaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison and crystallographic data.

claim: The HPD has high crystallographic B-factors in the BhYidC2 structure.
source: The tilt angle of the HPD also differs, as well as its side that faces the membrane (Video 1), which may be indicative of a high degree of flexibility of this domain, consistent with its high crystallographic B-factors (Kumazaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kumazaki et al., 2014.

claim: The HPD is not essential for YidC function in E. coli since the deletion of the entire domain is possible without compromising cell viability.
source: Notably, the HPD is not essential for YidC function in E. coli since the deletion of the entire domain is possible without compromising cell viability (Jiang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2003.

claim: In the structure of BhYidC2 a hydrophilic groove is formed on the cytoplasmic side of the TM bundle.
source: In the structure of BhYidC2 a hydrophilic groove is formed on the cytoplasmic side of the TM bundle that has been proposed to form a binding site for YidC substrates (Kumazaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kumazaki et al., 2014.

claim: The hydrophilic groove in BhYidC2 has been proposed to form a binding site for YidC substrates.
source: In the structure of BhYidC2 a hydrophilic groove is formed on the cytoplasmic side of the TM bundle that has been proposed to form a binding site for YidC substrates (Kumazaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kumazaki et al., 2014.

claim: The opening state of the hydrophilic groove differs between the two BhYidC2 crystal forms, being more open in 3WO6 than in 3WO7.
source: Interestingly, the opening state of this groove differs between the two crystal forms, that is it is more open in 3WO6 than in 3WO7 (Video 1), largely due to movement of the N-terminal half of TM3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the two crystal structures.

claim: The difference in groove opening between the two BhYidC2 crystal forms is largely due to movement of the N-terminal half of TM3.
source: Interestingly, the opening state of this groove differs between the two crystal forms, that is it is more open in 3WO6 than in 3WO7 (Video 1), largely due to movement of the N-terminal half of TM3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the two crystal structures.

claim: In the E. coli YidC model, the hydrophilic groove is even more closed than in BhYidC2 3WO7.
source: In our model on the other hand, this hydrophilic groove is even more closed than in 3WO7 because we imposed covariation-based constraints between TM3 and TM5 (Pro425-Pro499) and between TM3 and TM6 (Cys423-Gln528 & Phe433-Thr524) (Figure 2; Video 1).
evidence: This is based on the structural modeling with covariation constraints.

claim: Covariation-based constraints were imposed between TM3 and TM5 (Pro425-Pro499) and between TM3 and TM6 (Cys423-Gln528 & Phe433-Thr524) in the E. coli YidC model.
source: In our model on the other hand, this hydrophilic groove is even more closed than in 3WO7 because we imposed covariation-based constraints between TM3 and TM5 (Pro425-Pro499) and between TM3 and TM6 (Cys423-Gln528 & Phe433-Thr524) (Figure 2; Video 1).
evidence: This is based on the structural modeling procedure.

claim: In BhYidC2 the distances between the Cβ atoms of the three covariation-predicted pairs (Pro425-Pro499, Cys423-Gln528, Phe433-Thr524) are outliers compared to other residue–residue pairs (20.5 Å/20.9 Å/14.9 Å vs an average of 8.2 Å).
source: Strikingly, in BhYidC2 the distances between the Cβ atoms of these three pairs are outliers compared to other residue–residue pairs (20.5 Å/20.9 Å/14.9 Å vs an average of 8.2 Å, Table 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure and covariation predictions.

claim: Movement of TM3 is a genuine feature of YidC.
source: Thus, given that (i) the position of TM3 differs in the two crystal forms, and (ii) that covariation analysis predicts with high accuracy a closer interaction of TM3 with TM6 and one contact with TM5, we conclude that movement of TM3 is a genuine feature of YidC.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the crystal structures and covariation analysis.

claim: Movement of TM3 and the accompanying dynamics of the hydrophilic groove may represent a crucial step in the functional cycle of the YidC insertase.
source: This movement and the accompanying dynamics of the hydrophilic groove may represent a crucial step in the functional cycle of the YidC insertase.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observations.

claim: The YidC model was found to be very stable during molecular dynamics simulation.
source: Overall, the model was found to be very stable during the simulation.
evidence: This is based on the MD simulation results.

claim: The five TM helices enable a rigid protein core in YidC.
source: While the five TM helices enable a rigid protein core, the polar loop regions tend to swim on the membrane surface (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on the MD simulation results.

claim: The polar loop regions of YidC tend to swim on the membrane surface.
source: While the five TM helices enable a rigid protein core, the polar loop regions tend to swim on the membrane surface (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on the MD simulation results.

claim: Hydrophobic residues on the exterior of the TM bundle stabilize interactions with the apolar lipid tails.
source: An analysis of inter-residue interactions within the TM region (Figure 3B) provides a firm basis to the observed stability of YidC: hydrophobic residues on the exterior of the TM bundle stabilize interactions with the apolar lipid tails.
evidence: This is based on the MD simulation analysis.

claim: The YidC core is stabilized both via short and long-range interactions between the five helices.
source: The YidC core, in turn, is stabilized both via short and long-range interactions between the five helices.
evidence: This is based on the MD simulation analysis.

claim: Residues towards the cytoplasmic side of the YidC core are primarily polar or charged and engaged in strong electrostatic or charge–dipole interactions.
source: Residues towards the cytoplasmic side of the core are primarily polar or charged and, therefore, engaged in strong electrostatic or charge–dipole interactions.
evidence: This is based on the MD simulation analysis.

claim: Residues on the periplasmic side of the YidC core are primarily aromatic and involved in stacking and other nonpolar dispersion interactions.
source: In contrast, residues on the periplasmic side are primarily aromatic and involved in stacking and other nonpolar dispersion interactions.
evidence: This is based on the MD simulation analysis.

claim: YidC mutants T362A (TM2) and Y517A (TM6) completely inactivated YidC when mutated to alanine.
source: Some of the most stabilizing residues, T362 in TM2 and Y517 in TM6, both of which are located at the same height in the membrane, completely inactivated YidC when mutated to alanine (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the in vivo complementation assay.

claim: T362 and Y517 are located at the same height in the membrane.
source: Some of the most stabilizing residues, T362 in TM2 and Y517 in TM6, both of which are located at the same height in the membrane, completely inactivated YidC when mutated to alanine (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the structural model.

claim: YidC mutants T362A and Y517A were stably expressed.
source: Both mutants were stably expressed, indicating that the lack of complementation was not caused by instability of YidC (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on Western blot analysis.

claim: The lack of complementation in T362A and Y517A mutants was not caused by instability of YidC.
source: Both mutants were stably expressed, indicating that the lack of complementation was not caused by instability of YidC (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the Western blot data.

claim: Several residues close to T362 and Y517 show intermediate activity levels (F433, M471 and F505).
source: Several residues close to this pair show intermediate activity levels (F433, M471 and F505), whereas residues further away do not show an effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the in vivo complementation assay.

claim: Residues further away from T362 and Y517 do not show an effect on YidC activity.
source: Several residues close to this pair show intermediate activity levels (F433, M471 and F505), whereas residues further away do not show an effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the in vivo complementation assay.

claim: YidC induces thinning of the lipid bilayer during MD simulation.
source: Interestingly, we observed that YidC induces thinning of the lipid bilayer during the MD simulation.
evidence: This is based on the MD simulation results.

claim: A significant thinning of 7–10 Å results from the hydrophobic mismatch between the TM helices and the membrane.
source: A significant thinning of 7–10 Å results from the hydrophobic mismatch between the TM helices and the membrane (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on the MD simulation results.

claim: The thinning of the membrane is similar in the upper and lower leaflet.
source: The thinning is similar in the upper and lower leaflet, and the thinnest region is in proximity of TM3 and TM5.
evidence: This is based on the MD simulation results.

claim: The thinnest region of the membrane is in proximity of TM3 and TM5.
source: The thinning is similar in the upper and lower leaflet, and the thinnest region is in proximity of TM3 and TM5.
evidence: This is based on the MD simulation results.

claim: Membrane inserting YidC substrates have been chemically cross-linked to both TM3 and TM5.
source: Since membrane inserting YidC substrates have been chemically cross-linked to both these helices (Klenner et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2008; Klenner and Kuhn, 2012), we argue that thinning of this region in particular may be relevant for the molecular mechanism of YidC-dependent membrane insertion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Thinning of the region near TM3 and TM5 may be relevant for the molecular mechanism of YidC-dependent membrane insertion.
source: Since membrane inserting YidC substrates have been chemically cross-linked to both these helices (Klenner et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2008; Klenner and Kuhn, 2012), we argue that thinning of this region in particular may be relevant for the molecular mechanism of YidC-dependent membrane insertion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MD simulation and cross-linking data.

claim: A hydrophilic environment exists on the cytoplasmic side of the YidC TM bundle.
source: In addition, the distribution of hydrophilic and hydrophobic residues within YidC revealed the presence of a hydrophilic environment on the cytoplasmic side of the YidC TM bundle (Figure 3F), which continues into the mentioned hydrophobic cluster of aromatic residues towards the periplasmic side.
evidence: This is based on the MD simulation analysis.

claim: The hydrophilic environment on the cytoplasmic side of YidC continues into a hydrophobic cluster of aromatic residues towards the periplasmic side.
source: In addition, the distribution of hydrophilic and hydrophobic residues within YidC revealed the presence of a hydrophilic environment on the cytoplasmic side of the YidC TM bundle (Figure 3F), which continues into the mentioned hydrophobic cluster of aromatic residues towards the periplasmic side.
evidence: This is based on the MD simulation analysis.

claim: The hydrophilic environment in YidC may receive the polar termini and loops of YidC substrates during the initiation of translocation.
source: It is tempting to speculate that this hydrophilic environment may receive the polar termini and loops of YidC substrates during the initiation of translocation, thus facilitating their transfer across the hydrophobic core of the (thinned) lipid bilayer (see below).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural features.

claim: Essentially the same conclusions about YidC mechanism have been drawn on the basis of the BhYidC2 crystal structures and accompanying cross-linking studies.
source: Notably, essentially the same conclusions have been drawn on the basis of the BhYidC2 crystal structures and accompanying cross-linking studies (Kumazaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kumazaki et al., 2014.

claim: Purified full length YidC (extended with the C-terminus of R. baltica YidC) was reconstituted with ribosome nascent chains (RNCs) exposing the first TM helix of FOc.
source: In order to provide a molecular model of YidC in its active state, we reconstituted purified full length YidC (extended with the C-terminus of R. baltica YidC [Seitl et al., 2014]) with ribosome nascent chains (RNCs) exposing the first TM helix of FOc, and subjected the complex to cryo-EM and single particle analysis to a resolution of ∼8 Å (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is based on the experimental procedure described.

claim: The YidC-RNC complex was subjected to cryo-EM and single particle analysis to a resolution of ∼8 Å.
source: In order to provide a molecular model of YidC in its active state, we reconstituted purified full length YidC (extended with the C-terminus of R. baltica YidC [Seitl et al., 2014]) with ribosome nascent chains (RNCs) exposing the first TM helix of FOc, and subjected the complex to cryo-EM and single particle analysis to a resolution of ∼8 Å (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM analysis.

claim: YidC binds to the ribosomal exit site.
source: In agreement with previous structural studies (Kohler et al., 2009; Seitl et al., 2014), YidC binds to the ribosomal exit site, however, the improved resolution now allows for a more detailed interpretation.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The weaker electron density of the detergent micelle was separated from that of YidC.
source: Firstly, we were able to separate the weaker electron density of the detergent micelle from that of YidC (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The presence of elongated structural features allowed docking of the YidC model in a distinct orientation (cross correlation coefficient 0.865).
source: Secondly, the presence of elongated structural features (Figure 4D–F) allowed us to dock our molecular model in a distinct orientation (cross correlation coefficient 0.865).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM analysis and model docking.

claim: Two prominent densities in the membrane region remained unaccounted for after placement of the YidC-core model, one next to TM3 and one next to TM5.
source: Following placement of the YidC-core model, two prominent densities in the membrane region, one next to TM3 and one next to TM5, remained unaccounted for.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM analysis and model docking.

claim: YidC substrates are known to crosslink to TM3.
source: Given that (i) YidC substrates are known to crosslink to TM3 (Klenner et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2008; Klenner and Kuhn, 2012), and (ii) that the density neighboring TM3 is aligned with the ribosomal exit tunnel and (iii) that at the same relative position nascent chains have been observed inside the SecY channel (Frauenfeld et al., 2011) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the most plausible assignment to the density near TM3 appeared to be the TM helix of FOc.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The density neighboring TM3 is aligned with the ribosomal exit tunnel.
source: Given that (i) YidC substrates are known to crosslink to TM3 (Klenner et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2008; Klenner and Kuhn, 2012), and (ii) that the density neighboring TM3 is aligned with the ribosomal exit tunnel and (iii) that at the same relative position nascent chains have been observed inside the SecY channel (Frauenfeld et al., 2011) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the most plausible assignment to the density near TM3 appeared to be the TM helix of FOc.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: At the same relative position as the density near TM3, nascent chains have been observed inside the SecY channel.
source: Given that (i) YidC substrates are known to crosslink to TM3 (Klenner et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2008; Klenner and Kuhn, 2012), and (ii) that the density neighboring TM3 is aligned with the ribosomal exit tunnel and (iii) that at the same relative position nascent chains have been observed inside the SecY channel (Frauenfeld et al., 2011) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the most plausible assignment to the density near TM3 appeared to be the TM helix of FOc.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Frauenfeld et al., 2011.

claim: The most plausible assignment to the density near TM3 is the TM helix of FOc.
source: Given that (i) YidC substrates are known to crosslink to TM3 (Klenner et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2008; Klenner and Kuhn, 2012), and (ii) that the density neighboring TM3 is aligned with the ribosomal exit tunnel and (iii) that at the same relative position nascent chains have been observed inside the SecY channel (Frauenfeld et al., 2011) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the most plausible assignment to the density near TM3 appeared to be the TM helix of FOc.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Single cysteine mutants of YidC in TM3 (M430C and P431C) formed DTT-sensitive crosslinks with FOc(G23C) upon exposure to DTNB.
source: Upon exposure to the oxidator 5,5′-dithiobis-(2-nitrobenzoicacid) (DTNB), only in the TM3 mutants a DTT-sensitive ∼90 kDa product appeared that reacted with antibodies against the nascent chain (NC-tRNA∼30 kDa, Figure 4C) as well as YidC (∼60 kDa, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on the disulphide crosslinking experiment.

claim: The crosslink product represented the inserting FOc TM domain crosslinked to TM3 of YidC.
source: Thus, the adduct represented indeed the inserting FOc TM domain crosslinked to TM3 of YidC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the crosslinking experiment.

claim: YidC mutants with cysteines in TM5 (V500C and T503C) did not yield any crosslinks with FOc(G23C).
source: RNCs lacking a cysteine in the nascent chain (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) or YidC mutants with cysteines in TM5 did not yield any crosslinks (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on the disulphide crosslinking experiment.

claim: The unaccounted electron density next to TM3 represents the TM of the nascent chain.
source: Hence, we conclude that the unaccounted electron density next to TM3 represents the TM of the nascent chain, and that the density neighboring TM5 represents TM1 of YidC (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the crosslinking experiment and cryo-EM structure.

claim: The density neighboring TM5 represents TM1 of YidC.
source: Hence, we conclude that the unaccounted electron density next to TM3 represents the TM of the nascent chain, and that the density neighboring TM5 represents TM1 of YidC (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the crosslinking experiment and cryo-EM structure.

claim: The remaining unaccounted electron density in the periplasmic region is attributed to the P1 domain.
source: We attribute the remaining unaccounted electron density in the periplasmic region to the P1 domain; however, because it is substantially smaller than the crystal structure of P1, we did not include it in our molecular model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The P1 domain electron density is substantially smaller than the crystal structure of P1.
source: We attribute the remaining unaccounted electron density in the periplasmic region to the P1 domain; however, because it is substantially smaller than the crystal structure of P1, we did not include it in our molecular model.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Flexibility relative to the conserved membrane region of YidC is the most likely explanation for the smaller P1 domain density.
source: Flexibility relative to the conserved membrane region of YidC is the most likely explanation for this finding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: No density was observed for the HPD in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: YidC provides a hydrophilic environment within the membrane core for receiving the hydrophilic moieties (termini or loops) of a substrate.
source: Two principal findings of our work suggest how YidC may facilitate this process: (i) it provides a hydrophilic environment within the membrane core for receiving the hydrophilic moieties (termini or loops) of a substrate, and (ii) it reduces the thickness of the lipid bilayer: initial interaction of the hydrophilic moieties of YidC substrates with the hydrophilic environment of YidC would allow for a partial insertion into the membrane, while facilitating exposure of the hydrophobic TM domains to the hydrophobic core of the bilayer.
